entry.title: CMS Synthetic Data Project
entry.content:
As I’m reviewing old class notes and projects such as this one CMS LOS Prediction, I’m realizing that I always forget exactly what I did, and how much time it would save me to document more as I’m working. I also realized that I didn’t actually have justifications for some of the decisions I made regarding why I did what I did to handle my ZID (zero inflated data) problem. To that end, I did some surface level research on how ZID can be handled, and in doing so I believe that my methods were in line with what I found.

Below are general notes on what I actually did, and my reasoning behind the decisions I made.

Data Processing

- merged enrollment, inpatient, and drug encounter datasets into a master set
    - had to identify continuously enrolled beneficiaries
    - check for duplicated entries
    - ensure that every entry corresponded to a single beneficiary + encounter
- PCA
    - found the 3 principal components explained a majority of the variance in the data
- Based on my exploratory data analysis I believed that there were structurally different underlying processes that generated the lengths of stays
    - For example, a broken arm is a very different “underlying structural process” than being hit by a car and needing life-saving surgery. Because of this, the probability distributions of the lengths of stay for people with less serious injuries are very different than those for people with more severe injuries.
    - My initial thought was that there would be some kind of way to “rank” these different disease severities however I couldn’t find any pre-existing or official rankings online. In order to deal with this, I decided that instead of creating simple rankings, I would group the data into separate clusters, and then create an individual model for each of these groups. This would allow each model to incorporate the different levels of variability between each of the groups, and better predict the eventual length of stay. It also allowed the groupings to be based off of all the data, and not just disease severity. This is beneficial because it accounts for the fact that there are more variables that determine length of stay, than only what medical problem you have.
    - To create these groups, I wanted to let the data “speak for itself” and assume nothing about the characteristics of the data, so I PCA to ?consolidate? the variability, and then used kmeans clustering (unsupervised method) to create the groups of beneficiaries. Then I split the original dataset based on these group assignments and created a separate random forest regression model for each of the groups.
    - A type of zero inflated model that does not assume the existence of structural zero’s, but allows for their existence through the grouping.
        - If the structural zeros do exist, then it is assumed that one of the clustered groups would capture those zeros, and if they don’t exist, then the groups would also reflect that.
        - This model also makes no assumptions about the probability distribution of the occurrence of both structural and sampling zeros

If you read all of this, thank you, I really appreciate your time. Any feedback, suggestions or criticisms are always welcome. Please feel free to email me at lukewilsen45@gmail.com!

entry.title: CMS Synthetic Data Project
entry.content:
If you’ve managed to find your way to this post somehow, then thank you, because you actually took the time to look through my website!

One of the projects I’m working on right now is an analysis of the synthetic datasets that are released by the Center for Medicare and Medicaid services linked here. My main goal is to try to predict the length of stay based on demographic features (age, race, sex, state), total prescription drug payments, number of diagnoses within a given year, presence of end stage renal disease, admission facility type (ER, inpatient, … etc.) and the most interesting in my opinion, the principal diagnosis code. I’ve been experimenting with different sets of variables and different methods of variable transformation, and so far I’ve only run one simple linear regression model that with these results:

Model Performance Results

Test Set Results

| Metric | Value | |———|——–| | RMSLE | 0.4615 | | R² | 0.3084 | | MAE | 0.8965 | | MSE | 5.2422 |

Train Set Results

| Metric | Value | |———|——–| | RMSLE | 0.4200 | | R² | 0.3800 | | MAE | 0.8326 | | MSE | 4.6377 |

Model: Linear Regression - NoneType - 2016train-2017test

These don’t seem too bad to me, but this is synthetic data, and I’ve only run one model (thus violating the “no free lunch theorem”) so I’ve got a lot more modelling to do.

Training Data Choices

This is really what I wanted to write about, to try and clarify the ideas I have about this.

As far as I see it, there are at least a couple of differen ways of dividing the data into training and test sets.

  1. Ignore the patient-specific effects, and use the most recent year as the test-set, and all other data as the training set. The problem or question I have with this method, is that it treats each observation (which is defined by a beneficiary ID, specific claim ID, and year) as though they are entirely independent from all other observations in the data set which is a big (and incorrect) assumption to make. I also am concerned about how using patient specific metrics, i.e. average claims per year, or diagnoses in a specific year, would affect the conclusions that I could derive using this method of data seperation. This method feels as though I’m missing out on some kind of information, or as though I’m making an assumption I can’t but I’m not sure.

  2. Just use the previous year to predict the following year, i.e. use only data from 2016 to predict 2017. This method obviously leaves out so much data however, that I don’t think it’s worth it.

I think the first method is the most viable of the two, and I think the main assumption I’d be making with this method is that that the observations are independent in regards to patient ID and year.
